To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Drosha is a critical regulator of vascular morphogenesis; 2) DROSHA mutations are associated with HHT; and 3) Drosha regulates the TGF-beta/BMP pathway through miRNAs and direct protein interactions.

mice lacking Droha in the vascular endothelial cells (VECs) developed a vascular phenotype similar to hereditary hemorrhaic telangiectasia, a vascular disorder that is caused by mutations in genes that regulate TGF-β signaling.

mice and zebrafish lacking Drosha in vascular endothelium develop a vascular phenotype resembling hereditary hemorrhagic teleangiectasia, a human disease caused by mutations in genes encoding components of TGF- β signaling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Drosha as an important regulator of TGF-ß/BMP signaling in vascular morphogenesis and integrity.
the role of microRNA in vascular morphogenesis and vascular homeostasis.
the identification and functional characterization of novel genes and gene products that are critical for vascular development and function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Drosha mutations identified in HHT patients are loss-of-function alleles, and that the phenotypic similarities between Drosha-deficient mice and HHT patients are due to the loss of Drosha function.
Drosha is a novel regulator of vascular development and homeostasis and that Drosha dysfunction is a potential cause for HHT.
Drosha is an important regulator of vascular development and homeostasis, and that its inactivation is a novel cause of HHT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Drosha is essential for vascular integrity.

Drosha, an RNA-processing enzyme, is essential for vascular morphogenesis and maintenance of vascular integrity.

DROSHA mutations can be causative for HHT.
